HEADLINE: Other Passions
TEXT:
“When I wind down I spend hours looking at blogs, Instagram and reading interior magazines and books.”

When did your love for interiors begin?

My grandmother, my dad’s mum, she loved upholstery. She spent 25 years doing soft-furnishings courses at Midlands Technical College. She made everything herself. So I think that’s where it came from.

So can you upholster?

No, but she did teach me to sew and do all those other wonderful things.

How did you come to work with interiors designer Thomas Hamel [pictured above]? I believe you are his first and only Perth client.

When [my husband] Bruce bought our house [in 2016] we wanted to redecorate it but we agreed we would live in it for a couple of years first. I have always bought interior magazines; Belle and Vogue and Architectural Digest and all of those. I’ve always loved interiors, and so I’d seen Thomas’s work; I loved the eclectic nature of it. In a way, he can be quite traditional, but always having contemporary and collectable pieces. So nothing ever looked like it’s all just brand new. It was really beautifully pulled together.

Does this mean Thomas can be the bridge between your contemporary style and Bruce’s love for paintings by the likes of Frederick McCubbin?

Yes, Bruce loves impressionism. I love classical things too, but I like the mix of contemporary and antique and collectables.

Thomas worked at Parish-Hadley in New York and I have always loved ParishHadley. He works all around the world and Bruce and I love travelling and love things from different influences.

In 2017 you sold 60 per cent of your business to Quadrant Private Equity. Did that allow you to take your love of interiors to a new level? There’s a complete redo of your house under way.

Yes, I couldn’t have done it before. Well, actually the business was doing really well at that stage, so maybe.

You’ve got an Andy Warhol Grace Kelly print hanging proudly in a room with McCubbins and works by Arthur Streeton. What’s the story?

That was the first contemporary piece in the house. It’s a present from Bruce. He got Thomas to get it for me a couple of Christmases ago. To me, Gracy Kelly epitomises that elegance and iconic style. I love the colours in that Warhol. You know how you can get a lot of Warhols in prints and pop art? That one you never could. It was my favourite but there are only 225 in the world. I thought: typical, the one I love I can’t get. It’s significant because Bruce broke the mould from his Australian impressionist artists and bought me the beautiful Warhol.

How does your passion for interiors help you do your day job?

I think it’s about my relaxation from work.

At night, when I wind down I spend hours looking at blogs, Instagram and reading interior magazines and books. It’s not with an intent of ever using it, it’s just enjoyment.

That’s my escape, it’s disappearing into it.

Your office is probably one of the prettiest we’ve seen. Why was it important to have a beautiful office, complete with Gracie wallpaper design from Aerin Lauder’s walk-in robe?

People spend so much time at work and they are so dedicated. I don’t think beautiful things necessarily cost more, it’s the thought and the effort that goes into making them beautiful. Fitting out offices is expensive, regardless. Our old offices used to have leopard print on our pin-up boards behind our workstations.

Many bosses are grappling with getting employees back to the office. Should we think more about the interiors?

Absolutely. You can create environments people want to be in and feel good in, even if it’s just having an outdoor lunch area. The way we interact with our environment is really important. •

HEADLINE: The Wizard is Back
TEXT:
Goodbye Chocolate Forest Floor; hello Metropolis. We reveal the signature dessert that chef Martin Benn has created for his hotly anticipated new Society Restaurant in Melbourne.

D O NOT ATTEMPT THIS AT home. It is not a recipe for you to make, unless you’re completely mad. It is, however, a rare insight into the complexity and creativity – and chocolate – behind Melbourne’s newest and most original dessert. (The only thing you should make yourself, I suggest, is a reservation.) Background: In 2018, Martin Benn and Vicki Wild (pictured, below) stunned the food world by announcing the closure of their acclaimed Sydney restaurant, Sepia.

Benn’s creative, meticulous, original food had gained the highest accolade of three chef’s hats in the Good Food Guide for six consecutive years, and dishes such as his Chocolate Forest Floor had legions of fans.

The next announcement was a shock as well. The pair moved to Melbourne, linking up with restaurateur Chris Lucas who shared their ambition to create a new level of sophistication for Australian dining.

Then something came up.

“With the lockdown, I suddenly had time to look inwards, instead of outwards,” says Benn. “I wanted to make things that were new to me, and not familiar.”

On July 1 the trio will open Society Restaurant, promising multiple dining spaces and bars, 12-metre ceilings, an open terrace and spacious velvet booths.

“People want something special, they want to be looked after,” says Wild. “We want Society to transport them to another world for a couple of hours, before going back to reality. We love that about restaurants, and always have.”

THE METROPOLIS

CONCEPT

“Everyone wanted me to bring Sepia’s Chocolate Forest Floor to Melbourne,” says chef Martin Benn. “But at some point, you have to leave ideas behind.”

Instead, he referenced the same flavours – chocolate, anise, cherry – and built them into a glossy, gothic representation of the faceted glass exoskeleton of the building at 80 Collins Street that houses the new restaurant.

“I sourced the architectural plans from Woods Bagot, and Nicolas Georges of [chocolatier] Koko Black helped me find a firm in Belgium who could 3D-print the special moulds of the facade.”

No longer a natural, mystical, forest floor of crunch and cream, the dessert now references a tough, edgy, competitive urban jungle. Benn says it’s a response to the new world in which we live, and has called it Metropolis.

EQUIPMENT

You will need a spray gun, commercial blender, Thermomix, stand mixer, blast chiller, and the usual brigade of fine dining tools (silicon mats, palette knives), as well as a thorough knowledge of the terms chinois, bioron, anglaise, cremeux, chantilly and feuilletine.

INGREDIENTS

• Cherries • Yukari (salty-sour rice seasoning powder) • Shiso leaves • Agar agar • Fennel seeds • Valrhona Caramelia (35% cocoa butter solids) and Manjari (64%) chocolate • Cacao Barry Inaya (65%) and Blanc Satin chocolate • Callebaut gianduja (70%) chocolate cocoa butter • Cream • Butter • Sugar • Vanilla • Charcoal powder

METHOD

• To make a sour cherry gel, ferment one kilogram of cherries with yukari and salted shiso leaves for four days. Puree, and blend with agar agar, vacuuming out any air bubbles.

• For the praline crunch, crystallise 50 grams fennel seeds, and blitz. Make an aniseed praline with feuilletine (crisp wafer), gianduja and Inaya chocolate, praline paste and crystallised fennel, and rest in the blast chiller.

• Make a crème anglaise custard, and cool over ice. Warm the anglaise and emulsify into the Caramelia chocolate with sea salt flakes and whipped cream to form a milk chocolate mousse.

• Make a dry caramel, then add hot cream and glucose, and blend with butter to form a chocolate cremeux.

• Make a charcoal spray with satin white chocolate, cocoa butter and charcoal powder and transfer to the spray gun.

• To construct the chocolate mousse box, begin with a layer of the praline crunch. Follow with the cremeux, cherry gel, and milk chocolate mousse, leaving time for each layer to freeze in the blast chiller before applying the next. Cut into rectangles and spray with the charcoal cocoa butter. Place the multi-faceted chocolate shell on top and serve. It’s that simple. societyrestaurant.com •

HEADLINE: Back to the future
TEXT:
The winery that once caused a stir with its $100 merlot is doing it again.

ONE HUNDRED DOLLARS A bottle. Thirty years ago, this was a scandalous amount to charge for a new-release Australian wine. Not even Penfolds Grange, the country’s most famous red, had yet cracked the tonne.

So, in 1992, when then Yarra Yering winemaker Bailey Carrodus launched a straight merlot with a $100 price tag – four times as much as he was charging at the time for his flagship cabernet blend, Dry Red No.1 – there was a bit of a brouhaha in wine circles. Not least because Australia was still in the grip of the recession we had to have; most winemakers were slashing prices, not raising them.

“It certainly brought a bit of attention,” says current Yarra Yering winemaker Sarah Crowe (pictured). Three decades on, she says, long-time customers still recall the audacious release when they visit the cellar door: “‘A merlot for $100!’ they say. ‘It was outrageous! I bought two bottles.’” Crowe has just released her first straight merlot under the distinctive white Yarra Yering label since she took over as winemaker from Paul Bridgeman seven vintages ago (Dr Carrodus died in 2008). In a nice case of history repeating, Crowe’s 2019 merlot is also $100 a bottle (well, $105, to be precise). But now it’s one of the “cheaper” wines in the range: the top, black-label “Carrodus” wines from 2019 come with a $275 price tag. (Grange, meanwhile, is now close to crossing the $1000-a-bottle barrier.) This is the best line-up of Yarra Yering wines I think Crowe has released since she started at the winery. Early in her tenure, Crowe introduced changes to production at the highly regarded estate that brought the wines in line with modern trends: wholebunch ferments and carbonic maceration to freshen the fruit flavour profile in the reds, earlier bottling and earlier release for some of the lighter styles.

These changes resulted in quite a few delicious wines that I reviewed enthusiastically. But in some years and with some of the wines, while other critics raved, I felt that Crowe’s desire to finesse and fine-tune went a little too far: the wines were too pared-back, too reserved. They left me wanting more of the depth and generosity I associate with this vineyard.

In 2019, though, everything seems to have aligned at Yarra Yering. A hot, dry growing season; years of effort in the vineyard to improve soil quality and moisture retention and give the old, dry-grown vines some love; a deeper understanding of how to best handle the grapes in the winery. The wines are still elegant, yes, and very much an expression of what Crowe’s trying to achieve. But they also have a wonderful density and concentration of flavour.

I’m particularly impressed by the viognier and shiraz released under the top Carrodus label from 2019. Crowe tells me they come from neighbouring blocks of old, dry-grown vines: the good doctor was one of the first to plant viognier in Australia in the early 1980s and was a pioneer of the practice of adding some of the white variety to shiraz, to bring perfume to the red, inspired by the wines of Côte Rôtie in France. He planted it next to his original plot of shiraz, established in 1969.

But I keep coming back to Crowe’s 2019 merlot – partly perhaps because, like Yarra Yering’s long-time customers, I remember when Bailey Carrodus released his first. It’s a fantastic example of the grape, a testament to the quality of the vineyard, a benchmark for the variety in Australia. Yes, it may be $100 a bottle (OK, $105), but in the context of the other top Yarra Yering wines, and compared with the prices charged for top merlots from Bordeaux or California – not to mention the 1990 Yarra Yering merlot – it’s a bargain.

HEADLINE: Stern Words
TEXT:
Patek Philippe’s outspoken CEO on the latest models, the secrets to the brand’s success – and the ‘misstep’ of a competitor.

RATHER LIKE THE WATCHES HIS FAMILY-OWNED company produces, Thierry Stern stands apart from his contemporaries, avoiding the usual sales spiel and preferring the straight answer to the diplomatic dodge. I was reminded of this in April, talking to him after the launch of Patek Philippe’s 2021 novelties. Headed by a groundbreaking Linear Perpetual Calendar with the day, date and month shown in one line for the first time, there was also a fresh Nautilus in steel, now with a green dial, and a handsome Calatrava with Clous de Paris dial.

The Nautilus is one of a handful of watches that’s been almost impossible to get, something Stern sees as both a blessing and a curse. Determined the brand doesn’t become known for just one model, he’s deemed it will no longer be produced after this year.

Stern: “You don’t want to over-produce such a watch.

We made a lot of them and I think it’s enough. To protect the value of the watch you have to have the courage to say ‘stop’ [even] to a bestseller.”

As to what replaces it, Stern is undaunted. “You need to have, always, new ideas ... and this is something that we have at Patek, so I’m not scared about that. We are working today for 2037 on the movement side – that means that we already know everything that we are going to bring out until 2036.”

But don’t expect a radical departure from the mantra that’s served the brand so well – “limited product, very high-end, perfectly finished,” as Stern puts it.

“It has to be a mix ... different types of products, from those with a simple movement to the most complicated. All of them should rise together. There is no future for the high-end complicated watch if you don’t have a simple one.

Everything begins from that base – this is what our clients expect also. Not everybody’s ready to spend a million on a minute repeater, and even for your kids, you’re not going to offer them a million-dollar watch for their birthday when they are 18 or 20 years old.

[Whereas] you can wear a nice Aquanaut, a nice Calatrava every day.”

The reference to gifting a watch to junior is probably no accident given Patek’s famous advertising line – you don’t own a Patek, rather you pass it down to the next generation – which raises the question of a watch’s longevity.

Stern: “Today, for most brands, after 30 years it’s over. For me it’s too humiliating to think that – it’s important for people who have invested in Patek that we are able to repair a watch after 30, 50, a hundred years.”

Of the 2021 crop, Stern cites the Perpetual Calendar with its multiple date discs as the most challenging to bring to fruition. “My grandfather liked this kind of perpetual calendar [the linear display] – it was on a pocket watch at the time – and my father always talked about it.

“We were thinking about it since 2012 and the challenge was to keep it thin enough. I could do it because today we have metals, materials – some parts, very small and very efficient – that we would not have been able to [manufacture] five or 10 years ago.”

That said, Stern doesn’t see advances in metals applying to the cases of his watches, something common with other brands. “You cannot do everything. Specialise in what you like and what you are good at, and at Patek that is called platinum and steel.”

Nor will the company be looking at the kind of marketing collaboration increasingly relied on by competitors, such as Audemars Piguet’s controversial hook-up with Marvel comics for a Black Panther watch in April.

“I saw the watch,” says Stern. “I was a little bit sad for them because it shows that maybe they don’t have any more ideas. And they should have plenty of beautiful ideas. There is no limit, except stupidity. It’s not very good for a brand to do that, not at this level. They will sell it, but I don’t think it will help for the future.”

As for Patek’s path to success: “There’s no really big secret. You have to do something nice. I don’t like to say it’s a nice investment – it’s a watch that’s nice to wear.

“Yes, the value is going up and I’m happy to see that. But you have to have a great design. A very beautiful movement, and very efficient. You have to be accurate. It has to be very thin. It has to be beautiful. And that takes a lot of knowledge and work.”• Bani McSpedden is watch editor of The Australian Financial Review.

HEADLINE: Renovate is all
TEXT:
Architecture’s top prize acknowledges the role the profession can play in preserving the built environment.

For an arts centre in Dunkirk, for instance, they not only restored a derelict seven-storey concrete ship-building workshop, they mirrored it with an extension clad in clear polycarbonate panels to make a new complex that seems paradoxically delicate and robust.

In Bordeaux they revamped a biscuit factory to create an elegantly rudimentary private home; nearby they transformed a dour 1960s housing block containing 530 dwellings into a luminous matrix of winter gardens and open-air circulation zones, and all without displacing any of the families while work was taking place.

“We are really interested in this idea of transformation by addition,” says Lacaton. “Or expansion by superposition, you might say. We take every opportunity to work with what is already there.”

Vassal is categorical: “We should never demolish.”

For them the architect’s role is not to impose a vision from on high, but rather to work from within, with what’s already present: not just the structures, but the memories and lives embodied in them.

“Good architecture is open,” says Vassal. “Open to life, open to enhance the freedom of anyone, where anyone can do what they need to do. It should not be demonstrative or imposing, but familiar and useful with the ability to quietly support the life that will take place within.”

The pair met at architecture school in Bordeaux in the 1970s and began their careers in Niger where their first completed building was a hut and compound made from straw and branches. Semi-permanent, constantly added to and enhanced as it weathered, that simple structure would inform the doctrine of their award-winning practice. “Niger is one of the world’s poorest countries,” as Vassal points out, “the people are doing nearly everything with nothing, finding resources all the time, but with optimism, full of poetry and inventiveness.” The pair’s time there was, says Lacaton, “really a second school of architecture.”

Returning to France, they established their studio in Paris in the late 1980s, flying largely under the radar until they were commissioned to breathe new life into the highmodernist Musée Nationale d’Art Moderne building that, despite its stoically elegant facade, was a ruin inside.

The architects saw the potential of the towering concrete colonnades, grand stairways and massive industrial steel windows and their coup de génie was to not restore it, but simply to rationalise the interior program to make it even more legible as a beautiful ruin.

“We wanted to create porosity in this imposing modernist structure,” recalls Lacaton. “To consider this monument as actually a place to inhabit, like a town square.”

Since 1979, when the inaugural Pritzker Architecture Prize went to American architect Philip Johnson, the annual award has recognised avowed modernists, men devoted to imposing massive structures – embodying massive egos – on the earth. (There would be no female Pritzker laureate until Zaha Hadid in 2004.) The past few years, the Pritzker has shifted, as has public opinion about cities, buildings, communities and households. “This year, more than ever, we have felt that we are part of humankind as a whole,” says Chilean architect Alejandro Aravena, chair of the 2021 Pritzker Jury (and the 2016 laureate).

“Be it for health, political or social reasons, there is a need to build a sense of collectiveness. Like in any interconnected system, being fair to the environment, being fair to humanity, is being fair to the next generation. Lacaton and Vassal are radical in their delicacy and bold through their subtleness, balancing a respectful yet straightforward approach to the built environment.” •

HEADLINE: Club Class
TEXT:
GOLF – OR, AS MARK TWAIN liked to call it, a good walk spoiled – has never been a particularly stylish sport. In fact, veteran golf writer Richard Allen goes so far as to say that golf and fashion are contradictions in terms.

And yet, golf might just be becoming stylish. So stylish, in fact, that sweater vests, tailored slacks and golf caps could be emerging as trends. I know, it sounds a bit much, but I don’t make the rules.

It behoves me to say, before I go any further, that I know almost nothing about golf, so do forgive me if I mix up my par nines and my plus fours. One thing I do know is that it seems like the absolute daggiest, least active sport you could possibly choose to engage in.

Which is probably why fashion has steered clear of it for so long.

But the thing is, fashion does love sport. Fashion, for its part, borrows sport’s credibility and star status, while sport makes a virtue of fashion’s glamour – and, let’s face it, enormous commercial opportunities. You don’t have to win an NBA championship to wear a pair of Air Jordans, or live anywhere near the ocean to dress like a surfer (a theory girls from my extremely regional high school took to its very limits). You don’t even have to go to yoga to look like you do. Fashion, so entwined with identity, allows us to show our love of sport, whether we play or not.

So far, with a few notable exceptions – John Daly’s bold, colourful outfits and Jan Stephenson’s monochrome ’80s chic – golf has resisted fashion, which is ironic given that it has, arguably, the strictest dress code of any sport. But a new crop of companies, focused on the game’s younger players, is determined to change that, and the timing is right.

Singer Macklemore has just released a golf clothing range, meant to be worn on and off the green, called Bogey Boys (cute, no?). Byron Bay-based label Birds of Condor make ’80s-inspired hats, polo shirts and more. Malbon Golf, founded in California in 2017, cleverly adopts Gen Z parlance (they’re called “drops”, not collections) and makes clothing that both adheres to private club rules (which remain conservative) but is also, crucially, cool enough to wear off the course. Its models are straight outta GQ; its Instagram a tightly curated hipster paradise featuring weed-smoking players, bucket hats and what can only be described as course porn.

The leader of golf’s new style pack is one of its actual leaders, former world No.1 Brooks Koepka. Handsome, built like a tank and with teeth whiter than the game itself, Koepka cuts a stylish figure on the links, and established himself as a breakout fashion player when he wore a pair of Off-White x Nike Air Max 90s in 2019. The shoes were unreleased (they still are) and their very enigma lent Koepka a sense of cool that money can’t buy.

And it goes both ways – just as golf is getting more stylish from holes one to 18, its influence is also being felt beyond club gates. Mr Porter is set to release a golf-inspired range later this year. The site’s style director, Olie Arnold, says the sport has provided refuge during the pandemic, enticing “enthusiasts and novices alike”, giving it new blood on and off the course. Sweater vests, for instance, are everywhere this winter, from the catwalks of knitwear designer Margaret Howell, Hermès and Michael Kors, to the store windows of Country Road.

So why golf, and why now? For one, golf has received a COVID-19 boost like no other sport, thanks to its socially distanced nature. But could it be, too, that golf, with its country casual, gently elegant, conservative but not corporate style strikes the perfect note of postCOVID-19 dressing? Are tailored slacks not the very sartorial midpoint of suits and sweatpants? Are we all not extremely ready for the metaphorical 19th hole, for a shandy and a club sandwich, possibly even a slice of cake?

Obviously, we are. And while I personally may not be ready to dress like a golfer, I will happily take style cues from the caddies at the annual Augusta Par 3, who dress in regulation white boiler suits, which is about as daring as the sport gets. Head-to-toe white, on grass? Talk about a game changer. •

HEADLINE: Forecast
TEXT:
Back in the ’90s, young grafitti artist Brian Donnelly marked buildings in Manhattan and New Jersey with the tag KAWS because he liked the way the letters looked together. Now the exhibition KAWS: WHAT PARTY at the Brooklyn Museum traces his rise to becoming a force in the contemporary art world.

Included are monumental sculptures of the COMPANION character plus appropriated and altered American cartoons.

Until September 5, and online. brooklynmuseum.org

Coco Chanel, an avid follower of numerology, named her first perfume No.5 as she believed it would bring bonne chance. A century on, Patrice Leguéreau, director of Chanel’s Fine Jewellery Creation Studio, has produced a 123-piece high jewellery collection with showstopping precious gems to celebrate the world’s most famous fragrance. Each piece takes inspiration from the five elements of the perfume – the stopper, the bottle, the number five, the flower and the sillage (the trail of fragrance). chanel.com

Zero Halliburton created the aluminium suitcase in 1938.

The latest Zero collection, which was two years in the making, features a chassis with ball-bearing wheels and a scalloped grip handle for easy lifting, as well as concave edging with four deep-set channels to prevent dents and absorb shock. Available in four sizes and three finishes.

$2190. Huntleather.com

Roger Vivier has created a range of androgynous soft loafers in calfskin, patent and suede leather for its autumn-winter 22 collection. Featuring a flat leather sole with a hidden 10mm wedge, as well as a 10mm external heel height, it comes in two styles: a metallic RV-engraved square buckle or the mini Broche Vivier Swarovski strass buckle. $1690. rogervivier.com

Multi-award winning British perfume designer Azzi Glasser believes fragrance is “the sense that you cannot see or touch but purely and emotionally feel”. The Perfumer’s Story by Azzi is now available in Australia, featuring women’s, men’s and unisex fragrances, as well as candles, including Glasser’s signature fragrance, Sequoia Wood. Eau du parfum, $195. Bespoke atelier service by private appointment, £15,000.

theperfumersstory.com

HEADLINE: Net Zero: The Next Big Opportunity
TEXT:
A growing number of Rich Listers are investing in ways to make business more sustainable, and therefore more competitive – and profitable.

Y OU WOULDN’T KNOW IT TO LOOK AT THEM, but Alasdair MacLeod’s cows have a superpower.

They’re helping to save the planet.

MacLeod, the husband of Rich Lister Prudence MacLeod and the son-in-law of Rupert Murdoch, is the owner of Wilmot Cattle Company, which operates two farms in the New England district of northern NSW.

Over the past decade, the investor, entrepreneur and former News Corporation director has become a passionate advocate for regenerative farming, a practice that promotes the careful management of pastures – in his case guided by state-of-the-art technology – to improve efficiency and reduce environmental damage.

The process is good for cattle production but it also creates an increasingly valuable by-product. Better pasture management boosts the level of carbon sequestered in the soil of Wilmot’s farms. Once measured, this carbon can then be turned into carbon credits and sold via financial markets.

In January, the potential of MacLeod’s venture was recognised when Microsoft agreed to pay $500,000 for Wilmot’s carbon credits as part of the tech giant’s push to not only offset its current carbon emissions, but all the emissions it has ever created. It is the single biggest trade of carbon credits by an Australian farming business.

“We are now grazing cattle in such a way that they are not net emitters of carbon, they are net sequesters of carbon,” MacLeod explains from his own property in Yass in the NSW Southern Tablelands.

“Everyone around the world is telling us that we should stop eating meat because it’s bad for the environment. Well, we are now beginning to demonstrate that cattle, managed properly, can actually sequester carbon. And that’s quite exciting.”

It’s an experiment, at scale, for making farms part of the solution to tackling climate change. For MacLeod, it is only one example of why solving the challenge of decarbonisation could be capitalism’s greatest moment.

“For quite a long time the environmental movement has been saying: We’ve got to do something to save the world,” MacLeod says. “And at last worldwide capital is being deployed to actually make this happen.”

Rich Listers are among those grabbing the opportunities now. Iron ore magnate Andrew Forrest has perhaps the highest profile, having spent much of the past 12 months searching the world for partners in an ambitious plan to turn Fortescue Metals Group into a green energy powerhouse.

Forrest has also joined fellow billionaire and Atlassian cofounder Mike Cannon-Brookes as an investor in Sun Cable, a project that aims to deliver electricity to Singapore from a solar farm in the Northern Territory via an enormous 3700-kilometre undersea cable.

Cannon-Brookes is also an investor in green energy lender Brighte and solar start-up SunDrive. In March, both Cannon-Brookes and fellow Atlassian co-founder Scott Farquhar invested in Genex Power, an ASX-listed renewable energy venture.

Waste industry giants Ian Malouf and John Richards are developing waste-to-energy plants, while the Kahlbetzer family has invested in sustainable farming and waste-toenergy businesses. Ralph Sarich’s private investment vehicle Cape Bouvard Technologies is working to commercialise technology that would make electric vehicle batteries lighter and cheaper to build.

For billionaire Anthony Pratt, the fact that capital is now pouring into sustainability is no surprise. His late father, Richard, built Visy Industries into a packaging giant by harnessing the opportunity of turning waste into new products back in the late 1970s.

That core idea – turning trash into treasure – continues to drive the group. After buying the Australasian glass bottle manufacturing assets of United States group Owens-Illinois in July last year for almost $1 billion, Pratt immediately committed to spending a further $2 billion to help increase the recycled content in glass bottles in Australia from 30 per cent to 70 per cent within five years.

“We’ve been working at this for decades, so for us this is not Johnnycome-lately stuff – we are Johnny on the spot,” says Pratt over the phone from New York. “We’ve invested billions in it, and we’ve got to continue to invest billions in it.”

He emphasises that the family’s push into sustainability was built on economics, not environmentalism. Pratt snr hated waste and hated paying someone to take it away. Using recycled product raw material would help make Visy both more competitive and profitable.

When Anthony Pratt arrived in the US in the early 1990s to establish Visy’s American arm, he was stunned to find none of his competitors were recycling. Spotting a gap in the market, Pratt closed an existing factory in Georgia and built a replica of Visy’s recycling-oriented Australian plants.

Then he waited for 15 years while the recycling message slowly got through to US business. Former US vice-president Al Gore’s movie An Inconvenient Truth, released in 2006, shifted the dial. Later that year, retail giant Walmart introduced a sustainability scorecard for suppliers, with the use of recycled content prominent.

“As a result of that, customers were queuing up to deal with us,” Pratt says.

Visy, which has 6 per cent of the US cardboard box market and $US4 billion ($5.17 billion) in annual sales, is still the only box maker using 100 per cent recycled materials. Not only has Pratt built five of America’s largest mills using Visy’s recycled model, but he’s powering them with clean-energy plants that stand next to the factories.

“I believe that sustainability and commerciality are not in conflict,” Pratt says. “Because fundamentally, using a waste product is cheaper than using a virgin product.”

MacLeod’s dive into regenerative farming has similar capitalist origins. Following a shocking drought in the early 2000s, his goal was to save his farms, not the planet.

“Through bad management we created an economic crisis, we created an environmental crisis, we created an animal welfare crisis and – believe it or not – we created a human health crisis as well, because everyone who worked here was stressed,” MacLeod recalls.

“It was a perfect storm of crises. I looked at it and thought, there’s got to be a better way of doing this.”

While MacLeod and his team have spent the best part of a decade overhauling the management of Wilmot’s farms – improving ground cover, ensuring pastures get the right amount of rest – it’s only more recently that financial markets have latched on to the potential of soil carbon, leading to the Microsoft deal.

“Investors around the world are now talking about looking for investments that will deliver something over and above financial returns,” he says. “That’s what’s driving ASX-listed companies to say, we’ve got to find a solution to how we deliver shareholders financial returns, but also something else.”

The Stokes family’s Seven Group is an example: in February it announced industrial subsidiaries Coates and Westrac would reach net zero emissions by 2040. Chief executive Ryan Stokes says the target reflects a broader shift across industry and particularly the mining giants that buy Westrac trucks and diggers. Both BHP and Rio are targeting net zero emissions by 2050.

“We want to be a stronger partner with some of those customers who are very firm in those commitments,” Stokes says.

Goodman Group, the industrial property giant run by fellow Rich Lister Greg Goodman, is similarly scrambling to keep up with customers in the logistics sector who are demanding warehouses that not only meet the new requirements of the e-commerce boom, but are also greener.

Energy efficiency is vital; another strategy is to build multi-storey warehouses that have a smaller energy footprint. “These things are major moves and these moves are creating opportunities,” Goodman says.

Pratt cannily tapped the financial market’s hunger for green investments many years ago by striking so-called green bond deals – essentially 30-year loans linked to sustainability targets – with global pension funds, which continue to press hard on such issues. He believes 2021 has brought a new momentum to the movement.

In part this is driven from the top, with Pratt pointing to US President Joe Biden’s ambitious green agenda as a big catalyst for change. China is also aggressively tackling emissions – for example, it instantly shut down a raft of steel producers in March to curb emissions – while Europe has committed billions to post-COVID-19 decarbonisation projects and, like the US, is considering carbon tariffs. Locally, Prime Minister Scott Morrison has come close to committing to net zero emissions by 2050 – without quite getting there.

These changes are important, but Pratt also believes the momentum is coming from a more grassroots source: ordinary consumers.

Naturally enough, he sees this most clearly through the prism of the humble cardboard box. The changes the pandemic has brought to the way we live, work and particularly the way we now shop have made consumers only too aware of waste, Pratt says.

“The packaging ends up in someone’s house. When the consumer is receiving the box they are even more sustainability-conscious than if it was thrown in the back of a supermarket.”

This gets pushed up through the supply chain. Visy recently received a $US30 million order from a large online retailer for 100 per cent recycled bags and has experienced a boom in demand for its paper-based alternative to polystyrene.

Demand for greater recycled content in bottles is also surging from customers, such as drinks giants Diageo.

“They now rate sustainability in their top-three key performance indicators. It used to be a ‘nice-to-have’ but now it’s an essential KPI.”

What’s particularly fascinating about the preparedness of the wealthy to embrace sustainability is that in many cases, they are taking leaps of faith. MacLeod, for example, says soil carbon gives agriculture a chance to contribute to decarbonisation. But he concedes there is a lot more work to do to refine the concept and more effectively monetise it.

“There’s a big question mark around what the potential is for soil carbon in terms of the extent to which it can help us with our carbon accounts – but there’s a big question as to how much hydrogen can help us too,” MacLeod says. “The journey is very exciting in terms of what potentially might result from this.”

Pratt likes to use the analogy of a toboggan when describing Visy’s approach to sustainability – a toboggan starts slowly, but then builds more and more momentum.

He also provides an important reminder of how capitalism can underpin environmentalism. The man with a $20 billion fortune likes to stay paranoid by telling his family and his team that Visy is only ever two years from bankruptcy, from being wiped out by some new product that hasn’t been invented yet. The more sustainable he becomes, the more efficient Visy gets and the harder it can compete – then the less likely its cardboard boxes can be replaced in the market.

“Most people think you’ve got to choose between sustainability and profit, and that they somehow are enemies,” Pratt says. “I see them as mutually reinforcing.”

CARBON IS SO IL' S SECRET SAUCE

COULD THE SOLUTION TO THE agricultural sector’s decarbonisation challenge come from the land itself?

That’s the question being explored by Alasdair MacLeod’s Wilmot Cattle Company, which this year signed Australia’s biggest-ever deal to sell its soil carbon credits to tech giant Microsoft.

Soil is a natural store of carbon – there is more carbon in soil than in the atmosphere and all the world’s plant life combined – and regenerative farming has long focused on improving farm management to lift soil levels.

MacLeod joined the movement almost 20 years ago, following a terrible drought.

The focus at Wilmot’s properties is on ensuring ground cover across its pastures is maintained. Software is used to manage the amount of rest that the pastures receive.

“It’s about ensuring we’re maximising the productivity from our pasture while at the same time minimising any damage that we might be inflicting from overgrazing,” MacLeod explains.

The amount of carbon in Wilmot’s soil has more than doubled since 2012. The potential for soil carbon sequestration was further underlined last year when the federal government named it one of five priorities in its low-emissions technology road map.

MacLeod praises that decision, saying the level of interest in the potential for soil carbon has surged in the past 12 months. “There’s a big opportunity for agriculture to demonstrate it can be part of the solution rather than part of the problem.”

Soil sequestration does have its doubters though, and MacLeod is refreshingly honest about the amount of work still required to prove the technology, including actually measuring soil carbon levels.

“It is quite expensive to measure this accurately,” MacLeod says. “There’s enormous potential. The thing is, we don’t know enough about what the potential is.” •

HEADLINE: High Steaks
TEXT:
Keri Craig’s gowns defined an era, while Trevor Lee’s cattle fed half the country. Together they have forged a partnership worth north of $1 billion.

THE LEES CALL IT THE BLUE MILE. A NARROW, straight corridor (blue, obviously) that we’re walking down, occasionally shuffling into single file to make room for the stream of gumboot-wearing, blood-splattered employees sporting ninja-style headgear.

The pace is fairly brisk – the shift is about to stop for lunch, and cleaning is due to start. But we’re all dressed for it: Trevor Lee is in a puffer jacket and cowboy boots, a knife clipped to his belt after our photo shoot, and his wife, Keri Craig-Lee, wears knee-high flat boots, enormous pearls and knucklegrazing yellow and white diamond rings.

Within minutes, we arrive at the viewing area for the sealed-off boning room, which overlooks hundreds of people chopping and carving the hanging beef carcasses (“bodies”, Trevor calls them). “Do you want to see the kill room too?” he asks, after explaining there is barely a smell in the complex because of a negative pressure system he installed. The place is quiet as well, even out by the cattle yards where dozens of Black Angus await their fate. Lee says they’re calm because they are handled the same way from farm to abattoir. The yard has been laid out according to the principles of Dr Temple Grandin, the famous American animal behaviourist.

Walking through the Lees’ abattoir in the Brisbane suburb of Cannon Hill gives perspective of the scale of Australian Country Choice, (ACC) the family business built on an exclusive contract to supply steak, sausages, mince and more to supermarket chain Coles. Each year, the abattoir makes enough sausages, if placed end to end, to wrap around the Australian coastline. Yet the 40.5-hectare plot in the riverfront suburb is one of the family’s smallest holdings. The business also owns 34 cattle properties across Queensland, spanning 2.4 million hectares, with the capacity to run 300,000 cattle.

For one of the country’s largest landholders and biggest private beef suppliers, the Lees – ranked 102 on the Financial Review Rich List with a fortune of $1.16 billion – have a surprisingly low media profile.

Partly, they don’t want to be bigger than their customers, and Trevor, 71, is clearly happier away from the media.

“Should I tell her this?” he often asks his wife during our interview. “Perhaps not,” she answers more than once.

Keri Craig-Lee, 63, is a different story. She has a profile in her own right, and a glitzy one to boot. By 19, she had launched her eponymous fashion label, known for ruffles, taffeta and high glam. Later she opened three boutiques and Keri Craig was stocked in stores nationally. “It was always feminine ... a lot of pink,” she says. “They didn’t really date much except the big shoulders that we had in the ’80s.”

Craig-Lee designed Renate Blauel’s wedding dress when she married Elton John in 1984, and was the first designer to be inducted into the National Retail Association Hall of Fame in 1987 when she was just 28. In 2017, she received an Order of Australia for services to business and fashion, and the family still has the Keri Craig Emporium in Brisbane’s CBD.

What is less well known is her involvement in ACC through the years, from hosting dinner parties for Coles executives and helping sketch out the original ACC logo, through to weekly meetings about the business with the Lees’ four children, sitting on the board and being heavily involved in succession planning, which she dislikes. “It’s just about dying all the time,” she says with a theatrical groan. “Shocking.”

For the Lees, the success of ACC is a story that’s as much about their 35-year marriage as anything else. “A romance of biblical proportions,” Lee calls it.

TREVOR MET KERI AT A BIRTHDAY DINNER IN Brisbane. A self-described “sad sack” restarting life with two sons under five after a marriage breakdown, the then 36-yearold had agreed to go only because Keri would be there. He hadn’t yet met her, but she’d already made an impression.

The fashion designer had recently been up to Roma, where the Lee family owned the Brindley Park cattle station, to judge the fashions at the annual picnic races and beat the locals at poker. It was a coup – for the young Keri Craig and for the country town, which was reminded of the designer’s pull when the plane circled back to drop off her suitcases, which had been accidentally left on board.

The birthday dinner wasn’t the most spectacular start for a great love story, but Keri later agreed that Trevor could call her. He did, asking her out to dinner with a day’s notice, and took her to The Fountain Room in Brisbane, where they would one day hold their wedding. The next date was tennis with friends, followed by lamb chops with the boys and mashed-together peas, potato and pumpkin. “All together!” recalls Keri with a laugh. It was a whirlwind, and though they didn’t have their first kiss for three months, they were married as soon as Trevor’s divorce was finalised. Soon Keri was camping under the stars with Trevor and her two stepsons. “Keri Craig coming camping!” says Trevor, still clearly dazzled.

While Craig-Lee’s career was soaring as she built on her reputation as Brisbane’s best fashion export, so was Lee’s. He had come a long way from being the uninspired school student sent to work as a jackaroo and spending too much time surfing breaks at Byron Bay and Noosa.

“I decided I really liked the bush, but I found it difficult to see a future there because there were so many impediments to how you can make money.” Lee’s father, Norm – a minister in Joh Bjelke-Petersen’s government known as “Gravel Guts” because of his Brisbane earthmoving business – bought an undeveloped property near Roma, and his son and a small team set about clearing it. Out on the tractor “eating dust”, 20-year-old Lee had time to think about what he needed to make cattle farming stack up.

It came down to doing more than just farming: he needed to turn the cattle into meat, and to find a customer. “That sent me down the train of developing Australia’s, and possibly the world’s, first vertically integrated model. Now it doesn’t sound like rocket science, but then no one was doing it.”

At the time, feedlotting – bringing cattle in to be fed on grain to fatten them up before selling them – wasn’t used in Australia. After his father had put out some feelers, Lee headed to Texas and Fat City, then the third-largest feedlot in the US. The concept – explained to Lee at length by a Texan with grooves in his cowboy boots from propping them up on his desk – made sense, and in 1968, Lee decided to give it a go with a 1000-head feedlot. But he still needed a customer, preferably one of the big supermarkets because export looked too daunting.

He couldn’t get to the supermarkets, but he struck a deal with major Coles supplier John Sturgeon. “I would say: ‘Every animal I produce for you will come to the same specification. Like cans of Coke.’ They said: ‘Mate, if you can do that, we will take 30 head a week from you’, which was a truckload.” Lee wasn’t the only one to have found feedlots, but he was among the first four in Australia, and the other three were focused firmly on exports.

By the time Lee was 23, he had been working around the meat industry for long enough to know something was up.

The Coles supply chain, he says, was corrupt. It looked to be a dead end until Lee was introduced to Coles management by an acquaintance he won’t name. In his first meeting with Coles, he laid out what was going on. At first, the supermarket giant was sceptical, but what Lee said was quickly firmed up.

“At that point I suffered many death threats and a few hidings. I got punched up. I had a revolver and still do. I took a revolver to work every day. It was a terrible scene,” he says.

“That was my intro to Coles and the top management.”

From there, backed by Coles, Lee’s business quickly grew, sticking to the two key mottos of “never not supply” and “never be too dear”. He hired more people, leased space to butcher the animals in the government-owned abattoir, and flew a single engine plane between Roma and Brisbane after being warned by the local police that they could no longer turn a blind eye to his speeding. He married, had two children, Anthony and Michael, then was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease, forcing him to slow down, eat better and delegate more.

After marrying Keri in 1986, Lee still hadn’t quite put the pieces together for his vertically integrated dream. He was expanding, borrowing to buy his own meatworks, and setting up anewbusinesswith apartner tolinkColeswithMcDonald’s, allowing him to sell more meat to Coles because the fast food chain would buy the trimmings or offcuts. Lee also got used to turning up to fashion shows and awards, and learnt to shrug off being called “Keri’s cattle baron” by the fashion pack.

Meanwhile Craig-Lee raced around Australia selling clothes and travelled to Hong Kong and China where her label’s fine knits and other pieces were manufactured. Life was busy.

However, one Christmas Eve, it looked as though their world was about to fall apart. The new sales partnership had been built on supplying Coles and McDonald’s but, as Lee now reflects, you can’t have two roosters in a henhouse.

McDonald’s wanted priority treatment over Coles, a move Lee resisted. Ultimately, the fast food chain and his partner seized control of the business and pushed Lee out. “It blew up sky-high. I was silly and naive enough to ring the bank and tell them that I was in trouble ... They closed overnight: cheques written Friday weren’t cleared Monday.”

Out of the ashes, and two years of court cases, ACC was born after Coles phoned its banker, National Australia Bank, and told it not to foreclose on the Lees. “He’s never been any different from the day we met, he’s very honest, and I think they knew that,” Craig-Lee says of Coles’ decision to back her husband. The supermarket, the bank and the meat man struck a partnership. Lee calls it a “tripartite agreement”, based on a fully transparent cost-plus arrangement that lasted for 20 of the business’ 50 years.

How did the rest of the industry react? “With that contract, I became very unpopular,” he says, leaving the impression it is an understatement. “It made sense to us, it didn’t make sense to anyone on the outside.”

After all, at one stage ACC supplied 85 per cent of Coles’ east coast beef, and Coles had paid for much of the expansion that ACC required to reach those levels. The Coles contract endured until 2017 when, as part of a legal settlement, the two companies agreed to part ways by June this year. By then, on the back of the Coles contract, the Lees had amassed 34 cattle properties and the abattoir, and were readying to lift their exports. In last year’s Rich List, Lee cracked the billionaire threshold for the first time.

FOR THE LEES, FAMILY AND BUSINESS OVERLAPS so often it can be hard to tell them apart. Craig-Lee’s parents live next door to Sutherland, the family house on Sutherland Avenue in Brisbane’s Ascot where the staff wear checked shirts with the house name embroidered in red block letters.

Undertaking renovations on site more than 15 years ago was the catalyst for Craig-Lee, who had considered taking her label to the US, to wind back her business commitments. “I started to ease out of going to the office every day ... That sort of changed me,” she says, reflecting on the transition from starting a label to being introduced by her parents to buyers, then manufacturing in Australia, and eventually China.

The Lees’ youngest son, Harrison, who is completing his third degree – a Masters in Finance – and is involved in a hemp seed-banking venture, also lives in the compound, although there’s no sign of him. The day of The Australian Financial Review Magazine photo shoot, a few drop sheets are hanging around the place – it’s being painted – and Craig-Lee apologises for the mess. She explains away some of it as a consequence of having Cartier, their 24-year-old daughter, staying for a few weeks. She is leaving that morning to fly back to New Zealand.

Sutherland features manicured gardens and art, “another passion”, says Craig-Lee, recalling the thrill of being at the New York auction when a Leonardo da Vinci record of $US450 million was set. There’s also a study with a gun cabinet and Murano glass guns, a fishing tackle room and a macaw that calls out “Trevor!” and “Shut the door!”. CraigLee’s mother, Dianne, is chasing after Pebbles the dog (which Craig-Lee explains is also the nickname for herself and Cartier, but there’s no time to ask why). The dog’s fringe is tied up in a black band, and we are whisked off to the Emporium in the CBD, trembling dog on lap.

In the store, the candles at the front display are selling well and, surprisingly, Dianne says, so are the cheesecloth cheapies on the back rack that her husband, Peter, insisted on. This all-in family involvement extends to the abattoir at Cannon Hill. On the day AFR Magazine visits, Lee’s sons, Michael and Anthony, are in their offices (one has hula hoops propped against the door, dropped off by Craig-Lee for the grandchildren after a clean-out) and are keen to get at least a few minutes with Lee to finalise some outstanding business.

The family often lunches together, and all dined the previous night after holding a 12-hour board meeting.

Indeed, Craig-Lee in part credits her successful marriage to the couple having similar family backgrounds: self-made, hardworking parents who brought their children into business very young. Craig-Lee, who admits she wasn’t a typical netball mum, and Dianne have helped nurture Cartier’s singing and acting ambitions, spending every school holidays in Los Angeles from the time Cartier was 13.

“I put an enormous amount of effort into Cartier’s career,” Craig-Lee says. “She couldn’t do it by herself, she was too young ... she just wanted to do it. Trevor and I said, ‘Let’s back that’.” It wasn’t all hard work and sifting through shonky agents. Craig-Lee recounts the time she asked Adam Levine, Maroon 5 lead singer and People magazine’s 2013 “Sexiest Man Alive”, to help her with the coffee machine. A cringing Cartier went up to apologise and introduce herself. “She said, ‘Hi, I’m called Cartier.’

And he said ‘I’m called Rolex’,” recalls Craig-Lee, with huge enjoyment. The family’s hard work paid off. Cartier, known as DJ Pebbles, has had two Billboard hits, was accepted into New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts and is now pursuing acting.

Clearly, any decision about the future of ACC after the end of the Coles relationship was a matter for the entire family. In fact, the Coles fallout was driven by discussions about succession planning, a potentially thorny issue given the next generation is aged between 22 and 41. Only the two eldest sons work in the business; Anthony is chief executive.

“Trevor would like the company to stay in the family, he would like it to go to the next generation. He hates selling things he likes,” says Craig-Lee. After 10 years considering the issue, the family has established rules of engagement for discussing business. Craig-Lee also holds weekly business catch-ups with each of the children. They’re trying out new things – if one sibling needs family capital for a business venture, all four children will have a share in that business.

“Anyone who says succession planning isn’t difficult hasn’t done it properly,” says Lee. “I’m still not sure we’ve got it completely right.” The process did identify that the time for relying on one customer had passed. “We started fighting with them; they’re bigger than we are,” says Lee, skipping over the acrimonous legal dispute with Coles around what constituted “exclusive” in relation to exporting meat offcuts.

With the Coles contract almost at an end, ACC is now supplying, butchering and processing for Woolworths and other retailers. It is also expanding its export market from China to Japan, America and other Asian ports, in addition to its own branded products. There is a focus on breeding wagyu beef, and discussions about branching into goats and sheep, as well as an investment in non-meat protein V2.

Succession planning, leaving behind their major customer, new markets, new products and a pandemic. To hear the Lees tell it, they’ve barely missed a beat. But equally, they seem laser-focused.

Ask them about whether they support Queensland’s lockdowns, and they prefer to talk about time spent on Stradbroke Island, where Craig-Lee decocrated mirrors using shells she collected on the beach.

What about employing Indigenous cattlemen? Or land management practices? On the former, it’s been tried but without much success, so now they support the Royal Flying Doctor Service instead. On the latter, any farmer worth his or her salt wants to look after the land, says Lee. They’re testing collars around cattle to replace fencing, and seaweed-based feed to reduce methane emissions. What about philanthropy?

The family does support medical research, and other causes, but would prefer to leave it at that.

One topic that clearly has their attention is a proposed 300-seat restaurant by the river, just near the abattoir. “It’s a problem,” says Lee. In addition to bringing extra traffic to the site, it might also curb long-term expansion plans, such as building another abattoir to butcher sheep or goats.

“The only reason we are cost competitive is because we reinvest every year,” says Lee, pointing out that in the past two years, the family has invested $45 million in the plant and, over the years, some $350 million worth of equipment. Being near the Port of Brisbane also means cattle livers being processed today can be in Japan by tomorrow.

But, as always, the Lees are fighting their corner and believe they’re doing it right. As for Coles, they’re sure the supermarket will regret its decision; they point out that few suppliers in Australia can meet the supermarkets’ needs, and Coles is now at the whim of volatile market pricing. In fact, they fully expect Coles will be buying cattle from them, and at a time when beef prices are soaring.

Either way, the next generation has Trevor and Keri’s back.

There was an initial reticence to do this interview, and CraigLee says she’s been burnt at least once by a journalist. Anthony and Michael appear uncertain as to why the Lees are taking the leap again; as the AFR Magazine leaves the abattoir, one of them jokes: “Don’t forget, we’ve got a rendering room.” •

HEADLINE: Son of One
TEXT:
After a decade of legal fights with his mother, John Hancock is making his own way in the world. And so far the returns are good.

I T WAS DECEMBER 2020, JOHN HANCOCK AND HIS family were checking into a hotel just outside of Dubai, and they were drawing attention. Not because anyone recognised him as the eldest child and only son of Australia’s richest person, Gina Rinehart. The problem was their luggage: along with suitcases, the Hancocks were hauling several pairs of snow skis.

It would have been, Hancock tellsThe Australian Financial Review Magazine, the first time someone had brought their skis to the sand dunes of Dubai.

With admirable perseverance, the Rinehart scion had been trying to take his family on a holiday to the slopes. The Hancocks live outside of London, and a wave of COVID-19 infections was causing countries to close their borders to the UK. Their usual haunt of Whistler in Canada was off limits.

Hancock, 45, booked an apartment in Zermatt, and then, on the eve of departure, their British Airways flight to Switzerland was cancelled. But he was not going to give up without a fight. That’s not the Hancock way.

With Dubai still open, and with his wife, Gemma, and three daughters Georgia, 14, Jasmine, 11 and Zara, 6, the family headed to the desert. From there he’d plot a way to get them to Switzerland.

Yet even billionaires have to suffer the disappointment of crushed travel plans. Unable to navigate the border closures in Europe, the skis were put into storage and the family took to the sun instead, holidaying in the Maldives. The double black-diamond ski runs that everyone in the family, except the six-year-old, can navigate would have to wait.

Mention the name John Hancock and most people think of the bitter courtroom brawl with Gina Rinehart over the family trust fund, which is now worth an estimated $9.2 billion. It will be a decade this September since his sister, Hope, first lobbed the legal grenade at their mother. Hancock and his other sister, Bianca, quickly joined the action. Ginia, the youngest, never joined in.

The Hope Margaret Hancock Trust had been established by their grandfather, Lang Hancock, in 1988. His grandchildren were to receive their share when Ginia turned 25. But their mother would warn them just before the trust was set to vest in 2011 they would be bankrupted if they took their money, due to capital gains taxes, and the only way to avoid bankruptcy was to extend the vesting date to 2068.

A courtroom battle has raged on, and is now in arbitration and mediation. And because of that, Hancock says he can’t really say that much about it. Despite billions of dollars being thrown off by the family company, Hancock Prospecting, the beneficiaries of the trust, the four children, have received just a fraction. And yet the payment of discretionary dividends (roughly $48 million each) in recent years has been important for Hancock. Along with a capital injection, and with a good deal of the legal heavy lifting done and the case largely in the hands of lawyers, he’s got the bandwidth to forge his own path, to step from the long shadows cast by a family saga that for so long captured so many headlines.

“For the first time in my life I had the ability to look after my family and also make decisions on investments,” Hancock says.

IT’S 1AM AND HANCOCK IS AT HOME IN THE UK, fumbling around for his phone that’s lying in bed between himself and Gemma, whom he married in the Pilbara in 2014. (Rinehart did not attend).

Most people who can’t sleep in the middle of the night attempt to practise meditation, or get a glass of water.

Hancock trades options. Or stocks. Or whatever he thinks he should be buying and selling after watching trading across European markets and then the US before he’d call it a night.

“I wake up around 1am and start tapping around the bed looking for the phone. Sometimes it wakes my wife and she’s understandably not impressed,” Hancock confesses. “My computer was forced onto the floor some time ago and recently my phone was banished there too.”

But the trades are, so far, paying off. For the first time, Hancock’s wealth has nosed ahead of his three siblings on the Financial Review Rich List. He’s ranked in 44th spot, with an estimated fortune of $2.4 billion. The wealth of each of his siblings is estimated at $90 million lower. Most of their fortune is tied up in the Hope Margaret Hancock Trust, which has a 23.45 per cent stake in Hancock Prospecting.

But Hancock is adding to his pile.

A year before the aborted trip to Switzerland, back in January 2020, Hancock was on a chairlift in Whistler, talking to Gavin Rezos, a friend and investment banker who’d also grown up in Perth.

As the lift zipped them up the mountain, Rezos told Hancock about a little-known company where he’d just become chairman, called Vulcan Energy. Listed on the ASX, but developing a project in Germany, it plans to develop zero-carbon lithium products to feed growing demand for electric vehicles.

“I was looking for an interesting project to get behind. I was ready to sell down my Rio shareholding for something more exciting,” Hancock says. “Vulcan was trading around 20¢ at that point and I put it on my watch list, and did some research. I’m kicking myself now that I didn’t buy then, but in May 2020 Vulcan raised at 40¢ and I backed it with $200,000.”

He would continue to hoover up stock for months to come, eventually grabbing a 5.2 per cent stake at an average price of $1.10. By mid-January, while Hancock was on his skiing-turned-sunbaking holiday, the Vulcan share price raced to a record $14.20. His $4 million investment was worth $65 million.

And then something weird happened. Just a day after it hit that intra-day high on January 19 and just four days after Hancock’s substantial stake was telegraphed to the ASX, the family company controlled by his mother swooped on a parcel of shares at $9.50 a piece. Hancock Prospecting would continue buying and by February, when Vulcan did an institutional placement, Rinehart leapfrogged Hancock on the register with a 6.7 per cent stake.

The first Hancock learnt of it was when the substantial holder notice was lodged. “I didn’t discuss Vulcan with her,” he says. “I’m sure they’d done the research and came to the conclusion I did almost a year earlier that Vulcan is the best positioned lithium play out there.” In fact, it is the best performing stock on the ASX All Ordinaries index over the past year.

Hancock reckons it’s not the first time his mother has followed his investment lead. In 2010, he was having lunch with Rinehart at Bangkok’s Peninsula Hotel. She told him she was eyeing The West Australian. He told her it was effectively “Stokesy’s” paper. The open register, he said, was actually Fairfax, the former owner of The Australian Financial Review, The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age.

“She quickly got on the phone and told Jay [Newby, a director at Hancock Prospecting] to buy Fairfax. She switched the trade,” he remembers.

Years earlier, Hancock had been urging her to be “a partner of choice” for Chinese companies looking to make investments in Australia. He suggested listed wine producer Treasury Wine Estates as a potential example. In the end she opted for cattle, but the strategy was the same: to find a deep-pocketed and well-connected Chinese joint-venture partner.

How is his relationship now with his mother? Hancock becomes prickly, describing it as “complex”. The topic is clearly off limits. I try another way in, by bringing up a book of recipes and stories by Rinehart that was published in 2019. In the book she recounts how John visits on Christmas Eve “to play carols on our piano for us and to join us for our Chrissie Eve turkey and plum pudding!” When asked about that, Hancock says he hasn’t spent Christmas with his mother for 12 years. I probe a bit more, knowing he doesn’t want this feature to be all about the family drama. Has she met his kids? Not the youngest, he replies, who’s six. He later recounts a story of having to borrow money from a friend to buy his house in Whistler. It was only when he received a large dividend payment about five years ago that he was able to repay the money.

And yet, in some ways he exudes similarities to his mother.

Take, for instance, his pride in his involvement with Snow Australia. Together with Jeff Easton, the managing partner of New York fund manager and venture capitalist firm The Lind Partners (where Hancock sits on an advisory board), he’s donated $500,000 “to help young Australians progress in a sport that has given our family so much”. The funds, he says, are helping foster future Olympic talent. His mother, of course, is a patron for Australia’s Olympic swimmers through her support for Swimming Australia.

Gina Rinehart is notoriously reluctant to be profiled. In 2018 she granted a rare interview to this magazine, but insisted on using her own photographer. For this article, Hancock insists on arranging his own photographer to take photos of him and his family in the Maldives.

In his interviews he prefers the safety of email. It was only after months of back and forth that he agreed to an interview via video.

And just like his mother, he heaps praise on the legacy of Lang Hancock, who with Peter Wright pegged vast tracts of the Pilbara and lobbied for their development in the 1950s and 1960s. Up until 1961, Australia had banned iron ore exports, a hangover from World War II.

“My grandfather’s dedication to the development of the Pilbara is probably the single most important force in modern Australia’s economic history,” Hancock says. “He dedicated 99 per cent of his time to trying to develop the Pilbara, iron ore and also other projects of grand vision, such as tidal power generation. The other 1 per cent was on politics. He didn’t really have hobbies or other interests other than flying his planes to more efficiently travel for his business.

“Bianca and I loved our many trips to the Pilbara with him, his capacity for grand vision, and I think she’d agree they form the core of who we now are.”

COMBINED, THE RINEHART FAMILY IS WORTH $40 billion. It makes them the richest family in the country. The next closest are the Pratts, worth half that at $20 billion.

John Hancock was born in 1976, the first child to Rinehart from her first marriage to Greg Hayward when she was 19. She’d have another child with him, Bianca, before they would separate when Hancock was four years old. In The House of Hancock, author Debi Marshall wrote that Hayward didn’t see his children for 20 years. Hancock ignores my questions about him.

In 1983, Rinehart married a man more than twice her age, 57-year-old US lawyer Frank Rinehart. He died in 1990, two years before her dad, Lang.

According to Adele Ferguson, in her 2012 book Gina Rinehart: the Untold Story of the Richest Woman in the World, Hancock felt that his younger sisters, Hope and Ginia, were “put on top from the moment they were born”. He describes his stepfather as a “hard man”. He would later drop his stepfather’s name, adopting his grandfather, Lang Hancock’s surname by deed poll.

Hancock attended Perth’s elite Christ Church Grammar School, where he was mates with another billionaire’s son, Ryan Stokes. He did a year of commerce in New Zealand followed by a couple of years at law school at Bond University on the Gold Coast. He worked for the family company, including a two-year stint in South Africa with its jointventure partner. Back in Perth in 2000, he’d go back to uni, this time completing an MBA at Notre Dame in 2003. He left Perth in 2015, initially for Whistler before basing himself in the UK in 2017.

But he keeps Western Australia close. On our video call I can see a huge painting of Prevelly Beach, in Margaret River, hanging in the living room. He tells me there are prints of the Pilbara hanging in his home too. In another room off the main living room is a print of Rottnest Island.

It’s a place of fond memories. He recalls a trip to Rottnest, about an hour’s ferry ride from Perth, with Kerry and Ryan Stokes. At one point Kerry reached under a ledge and caught a crayfish with his bare hands. “For a 12-year-old boy that pretty much sealed his status as super cool,” he says.

“After my grandfather, I thought Kerry [Stokes] was the coolest guy. In some ways more so, as Kerry was younger and enjoyed exciting sports like skiing and scuba diving and it was an introduction to life outside of iron ore.” It would be Stokes who’d give Hancock a taste for the media game, organising work experience when he was 15 at The Canberra Times, which Stokes owned at the time.

But Hancock wouldn’t pursue a career in media. Instead, he worked for the family company and went on trips with his mother to China. In the 1990s, China was vastly different to how it is today. He remembers seeing the gigantic Qingdao Port under construction and walking through run-down department stores that didn’t sell western products. The industrialisation that was about to make his family the wealthiest in Australia was yet to ignite.

Hancock’s knowledge of China would later put him into the orbit of the budding iron ore entrepreneur Andrew Forrest. In 2003, Forrest was in the early stages of putting together an ambitious project to smash open BHP and Rio Tinto’s long-held iron ore duopoly in the Pilbara. Rio pays Hancock Prospecting 2.5 per cent royalties for the ore mined on the company’s Pilbara leases.

Hancock had been freshly turfed from the family empire.

He recalls being called into his mother’s office one day – not too long after a resolution in the Rose Porteous affair in 2003 – and was told his services were no longer needed. His salary was cut off. So he turned up at Forrest’s home to talk about China and Forrest’s ambitions for breaking open the Pilbara.

As Hancock tells it, Forrest offered him a job that would have made him Fortescue’s third employee behind Forrest and ex-Rio executive Graeme Rowley, in exchange for what he recalls as 10 per cent equity in the company.

Knowing he’d be going to a competing company, he ran it past his mother. “I explained Andrew’s plans to develop a mine, rail and port and his offer. She made it very clear I was not to work for Andrew.” He suggested a joint venture perhaps, taking one of Hancock’s tenements and forming a joint venture.

“She wasn’t interested,” he says.

It’s the sort of sliding-doors moment to wince at.

Had he taken up Forrest’s offer, the equity he says he would have been offered would be worth more than $2 billion today.

But he did make a small profit on Fortescue. He bought some shares at 17¢, selling two days later, just before settlement was due. He sold at 21¢ and pocketed $4000. It’s not quite $2 billion, but it was something.

Hancock knows that back then he wouldn’t have held on to Fortescue for long. “I would’ve sold out way too early even if I had the money to hold on to the shares,” he admits. “They’d be worth $22 million now but that’s a lesson I’ve learnt. I’ve had the discipline not to sell the Vulcan stake.”

OF COURSE, IT’S NOT JUST HIS INVESTMENT in Vulcan that’s occupying his time. He’s been with The Lind Partners since 2014, where he provides background on Australian mining juniors, reviews projects and companies, and talks with its investors.

Its Lind Global Macro Fund is forecasting a net return of more than 200 per cent since its inception two years ago.

He’s dabbling in his own seed funding, backing – among other ventures – a hyperspectral drone company called EchoLabs.

Hancock also likes to keep fit and has an open water scuba diver licence. And he loves to ski.

Indeed, he appears to have an appetite for danger, even if it involves the potential for broken bones. He only avoids double-black runs because they give him vertigo.

But he confesses that his two eldest daughters are now better than him at skiing. They’ve participated in theWhistler athlete development program, a pathway taken by some Olympians. My inbox starts filling with images of his kids doing jumps that makes my jaw drop.

“I’m very proud of their achievements,” he says. “Apart from fitness and enjoying the mountain lifestyle, the girls have learnt a lot through skiing: how to manage risk, for example, with consequences of bad decisions being death.

Planning an attack on a tricky double-black and then skiing it is a life lesson in strategy and execution.”

Clearly, Hancock is no helicopter dad. •
